newsitem.title: USA: Shooting for par, noteholders sue Claridge Hotel.
newsitem.headline: Shooting for par, noteholders sue Claridge Hotel.

text.p: A committee of noteholders has sued Claridge Hotel & Casino Corp, seeking full redemption value of outstanding first mortgage notes, according to the group's counsel, Bressler, Amery & Ross, P.C.

The lawsuit stems from recent restructuring talks in which Claridge indicated it would not make a scheduled interest payment on the notes, sending the company into technical default this month, said Thane Carlston, senior vice president of Chanin & Co, the committee's financial advisor.

The committee is also pursuing full payment of the notes in the event Hilton Hotels Corp follows through with a proposed acquisition of Claridge. Hilton has proposed buying back the notes at less than face value.
Outstanding notes total $85 million, of which Hilton owns 35 percent to 40 percent.

"It's the committee's view that through further negotiations and sitting down across the table from Hilton, or anybody else, that this is a property that is worth more than a discount on the notes," Carlston told Reuters.

The lawsuit was filed on Friday in Superior Court, Newark, New Jersey. Oppenheimer & Co, which structured the note issue, was also named in the suit along with a Claridge operating company and real estate partnership.
Glenn Lillie, Claridge's vice president of marketing communications, acknowledged that the company knew of the lawsuit but has yet to be served with papers. He had no further comment.
Claridge announced on Friday it is involved in acquisition talks with Hilton. An acquisition by Hilton would be through a prepackaged bankruptcy plan, it said.

J. Louis Binder, the committee's chairman, said in a release "other" protection for individual noteholders is written into the indenture agreement. Specifically, he said there is a clause assuring that the payment of principal, any premium and interest will not be impaired or affected without consent of each noteholder.

The Hilton offer would buy the notes back at a premium to where they were trading before acquisition talks were made public, traders and analysts said. The Hilton offer would redeem the notes in the mid-70 price range, they added.
The notes traded into the mid-80s on Monday. One trader quoted an 81 bid, 82 offer on Tuesday.

Some analysts said a buyback in the 70s would be a good deal based on adjusted 12-month cash flow of less than $5.0 million for Claridge reported as of September 30. Chanin's Carlston conceded that earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) alone would not justify par recovery. But Carlston said the value should include millions more in "incremental cash flow dollars" and the property.
Binder said Hilton's offer was an encouraging development in the committee's ongoing efforts to negotiate a full recovery for noteholders, but that it was only a first step.
"The noteholders are in a strong bargaining position as they hold a mortgage on the underlying property, which is prime, strategically situated Atlantic City real estate," Binder said.
But because Hilton owns more than 1/3 of the notes, analysts said they can block any plan they don't like. In other words, Hilton is not obligated to pay at par.
The committee chairman added that the group is waiting for a response from the Claridge and Hilton.
Carlston said the committee is not currently talking to other prospective buyers.
